works.album: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55: I. Allegro con brio
tracks.label: I. Allegro con brio
tracks.local: media/Beethoven/Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55/01 Allegro con brio.mp3

notes.text: Composed mainly in 1803–04 with Napoleon in mind. When Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804, Beethoven reportedly tore the title page in half. It was published in 1806 as Sinfonia eroica.
Two sharp chords, then the cellos give out the theme. This vast movement grows from that plain rising arpeggio.
Near the end of the development a horn seems to come in early with the main theme under the violins: a famous ‘mistake’ that Beethoven meant.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55: II. Marcia funebre: Adagio assai
tracks.label: II. Marcia funebre: Adagio assai
tracks.local: media/Beethoven/Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55/02 Marcia funebre - Adagio assai.mp3

notes.text: A funeral march in C minor: a ternary march, large and amply developed, its main theme returning like a refrain.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55: III. Scherzo: Allegro vivace
tracks.label: III. Scherzo: Allegro vivace
tracks.local: media/Beethoven/Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55/03 Scherzo - Allegro vivace.mp3

notes.text: A lively scherzo. In the trio, listen for three horns: the first time a symphony had used three.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55: IV. Finale: Allegro molto
tracks.label: IV. Finale: Allegro molto
tracks.local: media/Beethoven/Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, Op. 55/04 Finale - Allegro molto.mp3

notes.text: The finale’s theme comes from Beethoven’s own ballet The Creatures of Prometheus, about the Titan who brought fire to humankind.

works.album: Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68

dream.credit: Portrait: C. Brasch, Berlin, 1889. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68: I. Un poco sostenuto – Allegro – Meno allegro
tracks.label: I. Un poco sostenuto – Allegro – Meno allegro
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68/01 Un poco sostenuto – Allegro – Meno allegro.mp3

notes.text: Brahms worked on this symphony for about 21 years, from sketches in 1855 to the premiere in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Hans von Bülow called it ‘Beethoven’s Tenth’.
The introduction climbs and falls against a pounding low C in the timpani, Brahms announcing his symphony under Beethoven’s shadow.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68: II. Andante sostenuto
tracks.label: II. Andante sostenuto
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68/02 Andante sostenuto.mp3

notes.text: A tender Andante in E major, far from C minor. Near the end a long violin solo recalls Beethoven’s late quartets and Missa Solemnis.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68: III. Un poco allegretto e grazioso
tracks.label: III. Un poco allegretto e grazioso
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68/03 Un poco allegretto e grazioso.mp3

notes.text: Instead of a Beethoven-style scherzo, a gentle intermezzo: ‘a little allegretto, graceful’.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68: IV. Adagio – Più andante – Allegro non troppo, ma con brio – Più allegro
tracks.label: IV. Adagio – Più andante – Allegro non troppo, ma con brio – Più allegro
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68/04 Adagio – Più andante – Allegro non troppo, ma con brio – Più allegro.mp3

notes.text: The horn call: in September 1868 Brahms sent this alphorn tune to Clara Schumann on a card. ‘Thus blew the shepherd’s horn today!’
Then the broad string tune of the Allegro. Its kinship with Beethoven’s ‘Ode to Joy’ is part of why it was called ‘Beethoven’s Tenth’.

tempo: Allegro non troppo, ma con brio

works.album: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73

dream.credit: Portrait: C. Brasch, Berlin, 1889. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73: I. Allegro non troppo
tracks.label: I. Allegro non troppo
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73/01 Allegro non troppo.mp3

notes.text: Written in summer 1877 at Pörtschach on the Wörthersee. Brahms told his publisher it was ‘so melancholy that you will not be able to bear it’. It is among his sunniest works.
It opens with a three-note turn in the low strings, answered by horns. Much of the symphony grows from it.
Violas and cellos now sing a second theme close to Brahms’s famous Lullaby.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73: II. Adagio non troppo
tracks.label: II. Adagio non troppo
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73/02 Adagio non troppo.mp3

notes.text: Adagio non troppo, in B major: the most searching movement, opening with a long, wandering cello melody.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73: III. Allegretto grazioso (quasi andantino)
tracks.label: III. Allegretto grazioso (quasi andantino)
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73/03 Allegretto grazioso (quasi andantino).mp3

notes.text: A gentle dance in G major led by the oboe, twice interrupted by quicker Presto episodes built from the same tune.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73: IV. Allegro con spirito
tracks.label: IV. Allegro con spirito
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 73/04 Allegro con spirito.mp3

notes.text: Allegro con spirito: it builds to a jubilant D-major ending, trombones and tuba blazing.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90: I. Allegro con brio
tracks.label: I. Allegro con brio
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90/01 Allegro con brio.mp3

notes.text: Written in summer 1883 at Wiesbaden. Brahms, 50 and a bachelor, called himself ‘Frei aber froh’, free but happy. Hans Richter premiered it in Vienna on 2 December 1883.
Listen for the motto F–A–F in the opening chords. It runs through the whole symphony, often read as Brahms’s ‘free but happy’.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90: II. Andante
tracks.label: II. Andante
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90/02 Andante.mp3

notes.text: A quiet Andante in C major, opening with clarinets and bassoons like a hymn.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90: III. Poco allegretto
tracks.label: III. Poco allegretto
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90/03 Poco allegretto.mp3

notes.text: Poco allegretto in C minor: the cellos sing one of Brahms’s best-known melodies, later taken up by the horn.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90: IV. Allegro
tracks.label: IV. Allegro
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90/04 Allegro.mp3

notes.text: The finale storms in F minor, then dissolves: the symphony ends quietly, the motto settling into F major.

works.album: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98

dream.credit: Portrait: C. Brasch, Berlin, 1889. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98: I. Allegro non troppo
tracks.label: I. Allegro non troppo
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98/01 Allegro non troppo.mp3

notes.text: Begun in 1884 at Mürzzuschlag in the Austrian Alps. Brahms conducted the premiere in Meiningen on 25 October 1885. It was his last symphony.
The violins open with a chain of falling thirds, sighing two notes at a time.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98: II. Andante moderato
tracks.label: II. Andante moderato
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98/02 Andante moderato.mp3

notes.text: Horns announce the theme in the old Phrygian church mode before the strings warm it into E major.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98: III. Allegro giocoso
tracks.label: III. Allegro giocoso
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98/03 Allegro giocoso.mp3

notes.text: The only scherzo-like movement in Brahms’s symphonies, and the only one with a triangle. Listen for it.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98: IV. Allegro energico e passionato
tracks.label: IV. Allegro energico e passionato
tracks.local: media/Brahms/Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98/04 Allegro energico e passionato.mp3

notes.text: A passacaglia: variations over a repeating theme that Brahms adapted from the closing chaconne of Bach’s cantata BWV 150.
The variations gather to their climax: the Baroque form carrying Brahms’s darkest symphonic ending.

works.album: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74

dream.credit: Portrait: Émile Reutlinger, 1888,[1] published 1904. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74: I. Adagio – Allegro non troppo
tracks.label: I. Adagio – Allegro non troppo
tracks.local: media/Tchaikovsky/Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74/01 Adagio – Allegro non troppo.mp3

notes.text: Written between February and August 1893 in a small house in Klin. Tchaikovsky conducted the premiere in Saint Petersburg nine days before he died.
It begins in near darkness: a lone bassoon, low, over divided double basses.
After the second theme fades almost to nothing, the full orchestra crashes in: one of the most startling entries in the symphonic repertoire.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74: II. Allegro con grazia
tracks.label: II. Allegro con grazia
tracks.local: media/Tchaikovsky/Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74/02 Allegro con grazia.mp3

notes.text: A waltz with five beats to the bar, described as ‘limping’: graceful, but never quite settling.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74: III. Allegro molto vivace
tracks.label: III. Allegro molto vivace
tracks.local: media/Tchaikovsky/Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74/03 Allegro molto vivace.mp3

notes.text: A playful scherzo that turns into a march and drives to a triumphant close.

tracks.title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74: IV. Finale: Adagio lamentoso
tracks.label: IV. Finale: Adagio lamentoso
tracks.local: media/Tchaikovsky/Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74/04 Finale - Adagio lamentoso.mp3

notes.text: Instead of a fast finale, an Adagio lamentoso. The symphony ends very quietly, sinking into the low strings.

notes.text: Written 1798–1800 on a commission from Prince Lobkowitz and published in 1801: the last of Beethoven’s first six quartets, composed in his late twenties in Vienna.
Allegro con brio: a quick, bright conversation tossed between first violin and cello.

tracks.label: II. Adagio ma non troppo

notes.text: A gentle Adagio in E-flat major, the quartet’s quietest movement.

tracks.title: String Quartet No. 6 in B-flat major, Op. 18 No. 6: III. Scherzo: Allegro
tracks.label: III. Scherzo: Allegro
tracks.local: media/Beethoven/String Quartet No. 6 in B-flat major, Op. 18 No. 6/03 Scherzo - Allegro.mp3

notes.text: A ‘tour de force of syncopation’: listen for accents that keep landing where the beat isn’t.

notes.text: ‘La Malinconia’, melancholy. Beethoven marked it to be played ‘with the greatest delicacy’. It alternates with a carefree dance until the two collide.

notes.text: Composed 1874–79 and first played in Saint Petersburg on 30 December 1880. Its subtitle, ‘On a theme of Beethoven’, comes from borrowings from the finale of Beethoven’s Op. 130.
Borodin was a professor of chemistry who composed in his spare time; this movement weaves in Beethoven’s theme.

The cello opens with a lyrical melody high in its register.

notes.text: Written in 1893 in Spillville, a Czech community in Iowa, on a summer break from New York. ‘Dear Papa Haydn kept appearing before my eyes,’ Dvořák said, ‘so it turned out so simple.’
The viola opens with the main theme over shimmering violins. The pentatonic scale, used throughout, gives the quartet its open sound.

tracks.label: II. Lento

tracks.label: III. Molto vivace
tracks.local: media/Dvořák/String Quartet No. 12 in F major, Op. 96/03 Molto vivace.mp3

notes.text: Listen for a high, interrupting strain in the first violin: a bird Dvořák heard in Spillville. He thought it a scarlet tanager; it may have been a vireo.

Allegro ma non troppo: a relaxed opening with a rocking, dance-like lilt.

notes.text: Completed on 14 January 1785, the last of the six quartets Mozart dedicated to Joseph Haydn.
The 22-bar slow introduction gave the ‘Dissonance’ its name: quiet repeated Cs in the cello, then harmonies strange enough that a critic complained in print in 1787.

dream.credit: Portrait: Unknown author. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Meditation on the Old Czech Chorale 'St. Wenceslas', Op. 35a
tracks.label: Meditation on the Old Czech Chorale 'St. Wenceslas', Op. 35a
tracks.local: media/Suk/Meditation on the Old Czech Chorale 'St. Wenceslas', Op. 35a/01 Meditation on the Old Czech Chorale 'St. Wenceslas'.mp3

notes.text: Written in 1914 as a patriotic piece on the old Czech chorale ‘St Wenceslas’, for string quartet or string orchestra. It became a wartime symbol of hope. Dedicated to Ferdinand Pečírka.
The chorale to the Czech patron saint builds to its fullest sound: in the war years, a hymn of hope.

tracks.label: I. Allegro moderato
tracks.local: media/Schubert/Piano Sonata in E-flat major, D. 568/01 Allegro moderato.mp3

notes.text: First drafted in D-flat major in June 1817, when Schubert was 20. He revised and finished it in E-flat; it was published in 1829, the year after his death.
Allegro moderato: a gentle, singing opening theme, unhurried even when it develops.

notes.text: Written in summer 1819 in Steyr, Upper Austria, and dedicated to 18-year-old Josephine von Koller, whom Schubert thought ‘very pretty’ and ‘a good pianist’.
Allegro moderato: one of Schubert’s most lyrical openings, a melody that seems to sing itself.

notes.text: Composed in February 1823, perhaps in response to the serious illness of the year before. It was not published until 1839, eleven years after his death.
Allegro giusto: bare octaves, stark and spacious, unlike the songful Schubert of earlier sonatas.

tracks.label: I. Allegro

notes.text: One of three sonatas written in the last months of Schubert’s life, finished in September 1828. He died that November, at 31.
The opening bars quote the theme of Beethoven’s 32 Variations in C minor. Schubert deeply admired Beethoven.

tracks.label: I. Allegro
tracks.local: media/Schubert/Piano Sonata in A major, D. 959/01 Allegro.mp3

notes.text: Written in 1828, the last year of Schubert’s life. When it was finally published in 1839, the dedication went to Robert Schumann, who had championed his music.
Allegro: a grand opening of full chords.

tracks.local: media/Schubert/Piano Sonata in A major, D. 959/02 Andantino.mp3

notes.text: Andantino, in F-sharp minor: a quiet, rocking song.
The middle section erupts: improvisatory, with harsh modulations, peaking in fortissimo chords.

dream.credit: Portrait: Elias Gottlob Haussmann, 1748. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tracks.title: Goldberg Variations in G major, BWV 988: Aria
tracks.label: Aria
tracks.local: media/Bach/Goldberg Variations in G major, BWV 988/01 Aria.mp3

notes.text: Published in 1741. Forkel’s 1802 biography says Bach wrote it for Count Kaiserling, whose insomnia young Goldberg soothed from an antechamber. Historians question the story.
The Aria also survives in the 1725 notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach. Its bass line, not its melody, carries all thirty variations.
